newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Socialists vow to keep all of France Telecom.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Socialists vow to keep all of France Telecom.

text.p: The opposition Socialists, taking a tough stand on privatisation before the French parliamentary election, said on Tuesday they would scrap the planned partial sale of France Telecom if they won power.

The party which polls suggest is gaining on the ruling centre-right before the May/June two-stage vote, would not proceed with the sale of 30 to 35 percent of the telecoms giant. This would mean "abandoning the principle of public service", Socialist spokesman Francois Hollande said.
The Socialists would maintain "100 percent public ownership" of France Telecom, the Post Office, power utility EDF-GDF and railway SNCF, Hollande said.
Reacting swiftly to the statements, Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said the government was counting on money from the France Telecom sale to recapitalise ailing state firms.
Analysts say the state could reap between 48 billion and 73.5 billion francs ($8.2-$12.6 billion) from the sale.
"The state has a duty to recapitalise these firms and we know big amounts are needed this year," Arthuis said. Among those due to get handouts are insurer GAN and arms maker GIAT.
The government has delayed the France Telecom sale, France's biggest ever stock market operation, until the election is over, but has promised to relaunch it on June 6.
After conservative President Jacques Chirac announced the snap vote, Socialist leader Lionel Jospin said he opposed privatising France Telecom, electronics firm Thomson-CSF and Air France.

But analysts had thought the Socialists were softening their stance after recent statements by party bosses. Former Socialist labour minister Martine Aubry said on Sunday the party did not want the state "to lose its majority in France Telecom".

One telecommunications analyst said not going ahead with France Telecom's partial sale would have little operational impact on the company. The government "was still going to be the main shareholder and nothing will change the fact it will face full competition when the European telecoms market is liberalised on January 1", he said.
It would also have no effect on the government's ability to meet the deficit criteria for joining a single European currency as privatisation revenues cannot be used to reduce the deficit.

The biggest implication of the party's privatisation stance was for the long-term health of the economy. "If you want the economy to move you need to oil the wheels and privatisation is clearly a big step toward that," said Sonja Gibbs of Nomura.

The Socialist platform was a far cry from the pro-market stance of Britain's Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair, economists said. But some suggested the party would have to move toward the centre if it won power when it found it had no room for manoeuvre room in the budget.
"This is not Tony Blair-style socialism committed to keeping the best of Thatcherism. This is not even soft capitalism. This is unreformed socialism," said Paul Horne of Smith Barney.
The French party's privatisation stand followed its announcement on Monday that it would scrap a law passed last February introducing private pension funds.
To lower record 12.8 percent unemployment, it has vowed to cut the work week to 35 hours from 39 with no loss of pay and create 700,000 jobs, half of them in the public sector.
The party's privatisation plank harks back to 1988 when late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand introduced the "ni-ni" doctrine of no more privatisations and no more nationalisations.
"Our philosphy is indeed the 'ni-ni' policy," said Pierre Moscovici, who helped to formulate the party's latest manifesto.

The Socialists backtracked on their anti-privatisation policy in 1991 under former prime minister Michel Rocard after the vast state-controlled sector was so starved of capital it needed access to private sector funds. He allowed firms to buy minority stakes in state-owned companies.
In 1993, when the centre-right took power in parliament, it launched a massive drive to sell off state companies.
Hollande said the Socialists did not rule out privatising firms which had no public service role, saying realism should be the guide. "We need to keep a certain flexibility" he said.
But he reiterated the party's opposition to privatisation of Thomson-CSF, adding the party would maintain public control of the defence industry.
He did not say whether the Socialists would proceed with the government's plans to privatise troubled state-owned bank Credit Lyonnais.
($ = 5.831 French Francs)
